utterances.text: Ljuban Andzic, who testified here on behalf of Miroslav Kvocka, said that the Omarska health centre had a stock of reserve medical supplies that lasted from the end of May to around the 15th of June. This is on page 7595 to 7596 of the transcript. And Mr. Andzic testified that after that when the members of the Omarska health centre went to the Omarska camp, they went empty-handed. Those were his words. Did you comment as to why his recollection is so different from yours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andzic is not a physician, and he had only very restricted access to medicines, almost no access whatsoever. What he could do was -- what he could have were various disinfectants and things like that. I don't even know why he spoke about such things because he's not a physician. He could not have access to medicines at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So even though Mr. Andzic was trained as a physician, he was not permitted to administer medicines at the Omarska Investigation Centre? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No, he is not a physician. He only completed the secondary medical school. He's a so-called medical technician, paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you see or did you get to know any physicians who were detained at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't remember their names. They were most -- it was the nurses who worked with me at the time who would tell me the names of those persons, but I forgot those names. I wasn't interested in them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection. Does the name Eso Sadikovic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard that name. Yes, he's a doctor, a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was he one of the physicians who you saw at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How about Dr. Jusuf Pasic, does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Enes Begic, does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: I think I heard that name but I cannot remember exactly at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has heard testimony that Dr. Sadikovic was last seen alive at the Omarska camp in 1992 in August of that year. Have you made any inquiries as to what might have happened to this former colleague?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that he's no longer alive. I didn't know his whereabouts. I didn't inquire about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Doctor, were you ever in the Keraterm Investigation Centre or camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you ever in the Trnopolje centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Masic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: Just a very brief question. Doctor, did you personally know Dr. Eso Sadikovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know any single person in Omarska until the day I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Masic. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dr. Gajic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have a question or two to ask you. You mentioned that the task of the guards was to sound out the detainees who needed medical assistance and to bring them to you. Were you allowed, you, yourself, to go around and see the people, the sick people in the centre, in the camp, the investigation centre, or you had to wait until they bring to you what they wanted to bring?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: I was permitted to go around. However, upon my arrival, people from various parts of the centre were already being brought to me. So we would start the work immediately, and the next guard would bring the next group and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you had no access to the rooms or to places where you can, you, yourself, find out who is sick or who is in pain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning I did, and that is what I was doing. However, the places were crowded. There were lots of sick and wounded people. Everybody needed something. They kept asking me lots of questions. I could have remained in one room for hours. And later on, I was just trying to reduce that pressure on myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This pressure because you were the only man, the only doctor for all the camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No. Other doctors visited the camp including Slavica Popovic, Nada Ljubic, Jasenka Mijatovic, and Vlado Radic, and others whom I don't remember because I had already gone. But I was the one who went there most. I was the regular one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And when you walked around the camp, did you see the conditions of living of the camp and how much they would affect the health of the detainees? Were you able to judge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: The conditions were extremely bad. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, we are not experts, but what do you mean by "bad," could you just try to indicate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: It was a rather small area with a great number of people. There were no adequate conditions provided for sleeping, bathing, changing of clothes, personal hygiene in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And according to you, what would this lead to after a while?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: These conditions, what would you expect to happen to people who live in such conditions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, of course such bad conditions additionally affected their health which deteriorated as a result of those conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What kind of epidemics would that lead to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: What kind of epidemics? Various infectious diseases, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Including enterocolitis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When some people are already sick, would it be sometimes fatal to live in such conditions for lack of medicine, people with heart disease, with such conditions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Doctor, you mentioned that you did have contact and conversations with the doctor at the epidemiology centre and that you thought that she did a good job of preventing serious epidemics. I'm wondering if you would give us an example of anything that was done at the camp to your knowledge along these preventive, epidemiological lines? I know somebody mentioned there was a place where they could dip their hands into before they went in to eat. But other than that, can you mention any measures that you're aware of that were taken to prevent epidemics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: One of the measures was a measure in the kitchen, before having meals, they would have to place their hands in a disinfectant. And also, I know that a vehicle with water came to wash down the compound. Then in the rooms, the rooms were disinfected. Other measures were undertaken in the kitchen itself. Persons working in the kitchen were also told to take extra measures, not contact any people with infectious diseases or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Were you aware, along these lines, of any accessible facilities for washing hands near the lavatories? We have had a great deal of testimony about many of the lavatories not working and that they were stopped up and various other unhealthy conditions. Were you aware of there being any measures taken? Because that would obviously be a source of infection for the kinds of diseases like enterocolitis that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, from time to time, the -- these areas would be stopped up but workers would come every day and try to prevent the sewage system from becoming clogged up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. In the course of your visits and your examination of the people that the guards brought to you, did you find some that were sufficiently seriously ill or injured that they needed to be treated in a medical facility such as a hospital and if so, what did -- were you able to do about those people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: For each individual for whom I considered that hospitalisation was necessary at that time, the Prijedor hospital, I would place that individual in the ambulance with the driver and nurse and send the person off to the health institution and hospitalise the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: What would you estimate, over the more than a month that you were providing these services, how many people, would you just estimate, roughly, you did put in the ambulance and see that they were sent to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: We kept a regular protocol. It's difficult for me to talk about figures. I can't remember exactly. But we sent at least 20 people off to a medical institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Twenty people in the period of something over a month that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: As I say, I don't know the exact figure, although it was recorded in the logbook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Was there any provision for you or somebody from the health centre being called in case of an emergency? I mean, you came, you tell us, on a fairly regular basis, but suppose somebody gets an attack of something serious in the middle of the night. Was there some access to emergency services when that happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: We were on call 24 hours, and in cases of that kind, we would go to the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did that, to your knowledge, happen very often? Did you make many such emergencies -- you or other people at the centre make any such emergency, unscheduled calls out there to treat these kinds of cases?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Emergencies? At least once a day, in addition to our regular visits, we would go to the camp at least one more time a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, some of the medicines that you listed, among which were stomach medicines, and obviously one of the problems we've heard much about were cases like diarrhea and various other things that can happen when people are crowded together and the hygienic facilities are not totally adequate. Were you -- in those kinds of cases, were you able to or did you make any recommendations to the people that ran the camp about special diets? I mean, we had lots of testimony that these people got one meal a day and it was -- the same meal was prepared and dished out to everyone. What did you do in cases of people who had diseases or conditions that required some kind of special dietary care?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as medicines for stomach problems are concerned, we treated people who had already had ulcers, being that -- people suffering from ulcer, and we had a list of those people and had medicines for things of that kind. For enterogastritis, we didn't have sufficient quantities of medicines, so we weren't always able to come to their assistance. As far as the food and the kitchens, we couldn't influence that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So if you did, as I'm somewhat familiar with this, if you did have a stomach condition, I think you as a doctor would probably agree, medicine can help but usually it's medicine in conjunction with some kind of dietary regime. So is it your testimony that you were not able to influence in any way the dietary regime of people who might have conditions that needed special diets?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Our only way out in situations of that kind would be to send the people to the Prijedor hospital. That's the only thing that we could do, and we did so in a few cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Did you treat some of the women detainees during the period you were there? Did you have some women patients as well as men? There were a much smaller number of women but we have been told there were somewhere in the area of 30 or 40 women there. Did you treat any of those?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: While I was there, as far as I know, there were two women, and I remember on one occasion one of those two women working in the kitchen had injured a finger and we had to give her first aid for the finger. That's the first time I saw that individual and never saw her again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you -- did you ever have occasion to treat any women for the effects of forced sexual intercourse or what might have been rape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that did not occur at all, but as I say, while I was there, there were two women, and they didn't come to me for a problem of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My last question to you is: As a physician, did you consider that the detainees at Omarska Investigation Centre were receiving adequate medical care? As an overall -- an overall conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: The medical care was not perhaps adequate at that time and under those conditions and circumstances, but it couldn't have been better, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: By professional medical standards with which you've been educated, is it fair to say you would not say, if asked straight out, were the people there receiving adequate medical care, you would not say yes, would you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: The people that came to me for help and who were able to -- for which we were able to come by medications, they were taken care of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No. I understand that, but as a doctor, and looking at it from patients' point of view, who have some medical conditions, and leaving out whether or not war conditions and war shortages and everything else might have explained or justified reasons why more fulsome care could not be given, would your conclusion still as a doctor be that these detainees, based on your observations, knowledge, over that month and a half, receiving adequate medical care?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, as a physician, it's very difficult to work without a laboratory and without all the other specialist aids and findings. At that time, that was quite inaccessible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Dr. Gajic, I too have at least four questions for you or four general lines of questions or areas. The first is the following: If you consider an injury and its cause, that is to say the cause of injury and the instruments used, could you tell us what was the general results of your observations? We know that patients, the prisoners, didn't like to say who beat them but your clinical examination and your clinical eye gave you the possibility of observing how a wound was inflicted, how an injury was inflicted. Could you tell us, generally speaking, how -- what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Most of the injuries occurred from blows with blunt instruments, including, for example, an army boot, then the butt of a rifle, hands, fists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Thank you. Another aspect relative to that same area, on the basis of your powers of observation, what would you say that the physical condition was of the people you observed, directly and in general, when you passed around, when you walked around? What was the physical condition of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the physical condition was fairly bad. People were tired, distraught, psychologically distraught. It was a sorry sight to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question for you, Dr. Gajic. You said that a number of physicians, if I understood you correctly, went to the investigation centre. How did you organise yourselves for doing the work you did there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, the work was organised in the following way: Every morning at about 7.30, I would stock up on medicaments and sanitary material in the pharmacy which was attached to the health centre. I would take all the medicines that I would need and sanitary material and then we had an ambulance, a military ambulance, the S-4 type of military ambulance, with four beds for the transport of injured persons and two sitting seats, and it would be a driver and two, one or two nurses would accompany the driver, depending on how many were free, could be -- were expendable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have, can I say, a calendar of your present -- of the presence of each doctor, a schedule, or did the physicians all arrive at the same time or did they have a schedule, according to which they would go to the centre?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Slavica Popovic was the head administrator of the health centre, and she would determine the scheduling and order in which the doctors visited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So you were there. You went to the centre on the basis of indications received by Dr. Slavica Popovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: The first morning visit, we knew that that's what we had to do first, that as soon as we got up, we would go to that first visit. So for that first visit, we didn't need an order or an indication from anybody. We knew that that was our job. As soon as we got all the medicines we needed, we would go straight to the centre for the morning visit. As for the other visits, they would be done on the basis of phone calls. If we were phoned up or if Dr. Slavica told us to go there, we would go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said, Dr. Gajic, that normally speaking, the guards were in charge of sounding out the needs of the detainees, and medical care for the detainees and that the guards would give in -- bring in the patients, the sick people, they would -- the guards would bring them for you to be able to do your work. Now, with your clinical examination, that is to say, with your powers of observation, could you tell us whether the guards were organised? Did they follow orders, or were they indicated to do what they did by anybody? What do you think about that, could you tell us on the basis of your observations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't notice with the guards that anybody issued them any orders and specified what they were to do, at least not during the time that I was present there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You've answered the question. You were not able to observe any kind of organisation. Very well. But did it seem to you that somebody was there to enforce discipline and organisation or was it completely disorganised?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was some organisation. It was not disorganised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. And now another question for you, Dr. Gajic. You, did your job in the throws of an ethnic conflict, and doctors always take the Hippocrates oath? Did you ever have a situation where a doctor refused to treat somebody of -- on the grounds of ethnicity? You are not going to denounce anybody, we don't want to hear any names, but do you know of that occurring, that a doctor refused to treat someone because of his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: Where I work today, there are people of different ethnicities, and in principle, I have never encountered anybody even who even gave thought to acting in that way. It never entered their mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said "entered their mind," did you -- what about action? Did you see anybody act in that way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So nobody did that ever; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN GAJIC
utterances.text: I said that I never saw anybody do -- act in that way. I was never present to see anybody act in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Dr. Gajic. Thank you very much for having come to the Tribunal, for answering all our questions. We wish you a pleasant journey back to your place of residence and success in your work. Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have completed the witnesses on our list for today, and I think that Ms. Somers was about to tender some exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I forgot. I do apologise, Ms. Susan Somers. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. These relate to documents which were identified during the testimony of Mr. Djukanovic. They are Prosecutor's 3/290 and 3/291. Both relevance and recognition, authenticity, I think, are established. We'd ask to have them moved into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The Defence does not object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the exhibits mentioned are admitted into evidence. We have no more witnesses for today and so we're going to adjourn on time. I should just like to inform the parties that pursuant to our oral decision of the 6th of October 2000 and the 10th of May 2001, that is to say, yesterday's decision, the Registry has informed us that in the interests of urgency of the case in the Chamber and the availability of the technical means, the Registry suggests the date of the 31st of May for the video conference. The registry proposes the 31st of May. Are there any objections or comments from the parties? Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As of this moment, Your Honour, there are none. We will speak to the witness and confirm, but I believe it should be fine. Thank you very much for notifying us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. As you know, we have a packed schedule and we had to decide that. What about the Defence? Mr. Jovan Simic. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you speaking on behalf of all the Defence counsel or just in your own name? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, in the name of all the Defence teams. We have no objection to the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Registry can take note of the fact that we have done everything in our power to have that conference held on the 31st of May. I don't think there are any other outstanding issues for today. May we just see how we stand with witnesses for Monday or possibly Tuesday. Mr. Jovan Simic, how do we stand, just to see whether I have the right piece of paper in front of me? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Probably not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to have it now. MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The first witness for Monday will be Mr. Mirko Jesic. The second witness -- I apologise, may I just take a moment to check. The next witness will be Milos Jankovic. The third witness is Momcilo Stojakovic, and I think -- I think those are the only witnesses we shall be calling, just those three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have an expert witness as well, don't we? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We have him on our list for Tuesday, the expert witness for Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Following those four witnesses, those four witnesses -- after those four witnesses, are we going to have the expert witness; is that right? MR. J. SIMIC: [Interpretation] We have one more witness that we intend to have on Tuesday, and he is Stojan Vuleta, and I thought that we would hear the expert witness last. utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just comment in the event that there is a -- I think that would be a bit difficult in the way we've set things up with our own people. SIMIC: [Interpretation] The order will not be changed. No, I'm sorry, the order has been changed so Vuleta Stojan will be heard -- anyway, the expert witness will be heard on Tuesday. We'll have the expert witness on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to wait and see. I know that Ms. Somers likes order and we do too, so we'll have to organise ourselves.
